title: Indian-American Amish Shah Faces Trump-Backed Jay Feely in Tight Arizona Race
excerpt: The emergency physician and former state legislator, once a Jets team doctor during Feely's playing days, is locked in a neck-and-neck fight for a swing seat that could decide control of the House.
body:
• Indian-American Democrat Amish Shah, an emergency physician and former Arizona legislator, faces Trump-backed former NFL kicker Jay Feely for Arizona's 1st Congressional District on November 3.
  • The two know each other from the New York Jets, where Shah was a team doctor during Feely's playing years.
  • GOP groups have spent more than $22 million backing Feely, a longtime friend and golf partner of President Donald Trump, in one of the closest House races in the country.
  • For voters in the district: an October 1 poll put Shah narrowly ahead, 44% to 42%, and the seat will help decide control of the U.S. House.

PHOENIX — Indian-American Democrat Amish Shah is in one of the tightest congressional races in the United States, facing Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker backed by President Donald Trump, for Arizona's 1st Congressional District in the November 3 general election.

The matchup carries an unusual personal history. Shah, an emergency room physician, served as a team doctor for the New York Jets during Feely's time with the team in 2008-09, Reuters reported. Feely, 50, played for six NFL teams, spent four seasons with the Arizona Cardinals and retired in the Phoenix area before moving into broadcasting and launching his campaign in 2025.

A Swing Seat That Could Decide the House

Arizona's 1st District covers part of north Phoenix along with Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, Fountain Hills and Cave Creek, plus the Salt River and Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation tribal reservations. Control of the House is at stake. Despite a Republican registration advantage — Republicans make up about 38% of registered voters, against 35% independent or other and just over 26% Democrats — the Cook Political Report rates the race 'lean Democratic' and Inside Elections calls it 'tilt Democratic', according to reporting cited by hi INDiA (IANS).

https://x.com/yespunjab/status/2113869999689585021

An October 1 FirstStrategic poll of 400 voters put Shah at 44% and Feely at 42%, with 14% unsure. Shah won the July 21 Democratic primary with 53.4% of the vote against Marlene Galan-Woods, while Feely won the Republican primary with 58.2% against Joseph Chaplik. The seat opened up after incumbent Republican David Schweikert ran for governor; Shah had lost to Schweikert by just 3.8 points in the same district in 2024.

"When I'm talking to the voters, what they have said to me clearly is they don't want them in CD-1."

— Amish Shah, on data centres in the district, at a Clean Elections debate

Trump's Favourite, and a Flood of Outside Money

Trump has known Feely for decades as a friend and golf partner and sees the former Cardinals kicker as a formidable candidate, Politico reported, citing Trump officials familiar with their relationship. Trump endorsed Feely in the primary, urged the longtime Gilbert resident to switch from the 5th District race to the 1st, and his allies are mounting a late push in the district. GOP groups have spent more than $22 million to boost Feely, much of it in the final weeks, and federal filings show heavy outside spending on both sides, including $5.72 million by the MAGA Inc.-funded Safety & Affordability PAC against Shah and $4.41 million by House Majority PAC against Feely.

Shah has raised about $5.65 million to Feely's $3.80 million through mid-October FEC filings. Pollster Marcus Dell'Artino told the Arizona Capitol Times that independent turnout is likely to decide it: if independents show up in big numbers, it favours Shah; if they do not, it favours Feely.

Health Care Versus the Trump Agenda — and a Data Centre Fight

Shah served five years in the Arizona state legislature after being elected to the state House in 2018. The son of Gujarati parents who immigrated from India in the 1960s, he has made medicine central to his platform, pledging to lower health care costs and the price of essential medications including insulin, to fight for abortion rights, and to protect Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid. Feely describes himself as pro-business and conservative, both fiscally and socially, and has backed the Trump agenda.

The sharpest recent clash came over data centres at a Clean Elections debate. Shah said voters in the district do not want new data centres there, pointing to Arizona's drought and pressure on ratepayers as applications multiply and power demand grows. Feely argued the facilities add about a billion dollars in revenue to the state, creating room to raise teacher pay, and accused Shah of hypocrisy for having voted as a legislator for tax credits that attracted data centres. Shah replied that artificial intelligence was not on the radar when that vote was taken.

The race is now a turnout contest ahead of the November 3 vote.
